source.title: The effect of fine-tuning on language model toxicity
source.authors: Will Hawkins; Brent D. Mittelstadt; Christopher Russell

record.tranche_reason: The study measures toxic-generation rates after fine-tuning, not refusal or compliance with harmful user requests, response-position KL, opening-token bypasses, safety localization in weights, or deepening safety training.
record.gate_note: The paper reports fine-tuning effects on toxicity, a related but different construct from the claim versions' harmful-request compliance and refusal behavior. Those results are recorded with versions ["none"]. References to other studies' findings are not recorded as results. Subset rates other than Total and Severe are omitted.
record.test_reason: The study measures the rate of hate-speech-classified completions on RealToxicityPrompts and CEB prompts after instruction-tuning, Dolly LoRA fine-tuning and community fine-tuning. It does not measure refusal of, or compliance with, harmful user requests. It also has no per-token KL, prefilling or decoding attacks, weight localization, or deepening training. Toxic continuation is a related but different construct from V2's harmful-request compliance. Its results therefore go under fits_no_version, not into version verdicts. The authors cite Qi et al. and others for the safety framing but do not test those findings.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that developer instruction-tuning reduces toxicity, that a small non-adversarial LoRA fine-tune can inadvertently undo this, and that community-tuned variants vary unpredictably. They call for evaluation before and after fine-tuning.
record.recipe_differences: This study applies one epoch of LoRA fine-tuning on Dolly and measures toxic-generation rates; it does not use harmful-example fine-tuning or evaluate refusal/compliance as in the cited safety-fine-tuning work.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported toxicity outcomes vary by model and prompt subset; community fine-tuning can increase or decrease rates, and the Llama-3.1 community-model total-rate comparisons are not credible while severe-subset differences are reported as credible.

fits_no_version.finding: Developer instruction-tuning lowered toxic-continuation rates in all four base/IT pairs, with credible Bayesian differences. One epoch of Dolly LoRA fine-tuning raised total toxicity by at least 2.5pp in five of six models (e.g. Gemma-2B-IT 1.1%→8.8%). Llama-2-7B-chat showed a negligible, non-credible change.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign-data LoRA fine-tuning of instruction-tuned small open models can raise hate-speech-classified toxic continuation rates, with model-dependent size.

fits_no_version.finding: Community-tuned Hugging Face variants show toxicity changes in both directions. On the Severe subset, Llama-3.1 Chinese-Chat rose and the German-tuned SauerkrautLM fell, both credibly. Neither total-rate difference was credible.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Community fine-tuning produces hard-to-predict, model- and prompt-subset-dependent toxicity changes.

record.problems: Toxicity is measured with an automated hate-speech classifier and is not harmful-request refusal or compliance. Community fine-tuning methods and datasets were not fully visible. The study focuses on relatively small open models and LoRA; the authors identify further model-size and fine-tuning-method comparisons as future work.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted Random, Race, Gender, Age, and Religion subset rates from Tables 1–3; retained Total and Severe outcomes, plus the reported Llama-3.1 community comparisons. These omitted subset results are toxicity outcomes rather than measures of the claim versions' refusal/compliance behavior.

untested.parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and harmful-request compliance are not tested.
Benign (Dolly) fine-tuning is applied, but harmful-request compliance and refusal are not measured. Only hate-speech toxicity of prompt continuations is measured.
Per-token KL across response positions is not measured.
Prefilling, suffixes and decoding attacks are not tested. All generations use greedy decoding.
Parameter or rank localization of safety is not tested.
Causes of shallowness are not tested. Forgetting is only speculated about as future work.

record.verdict_notes: Toxicity is scored by roberta-hate-speech-dynabench-r4 (threshold >0.5) on 50-token greedy continuations. This is a hate-speech measure, not a harmful-request refusal measure, so no row links to V2 even though the Dolly setup resembles Qi et al.'s benign fine-tuning. Severe-subset rates for community models other than the two Llama-3.1 variants are in Table 3 but not rowed; for example, Moxoff rose 6.3%→17.9% and chat_uncensored 7.8%→15.9%. These would only matter for fits_no_version. No verdict labels are given.

versions.untested_parts: Whether harmful fine-tuning examples increase compliance with harmful requests or remove refusals.
Whether benign fine-tuning raises harmful-request compliance or reduces refusal. Toxic-generation rates are not a measure of that behavior.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across response positions.
Prefilling, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as ways to bypass refusal.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety behavior to be shallow.
Training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens and its robustness.
